{"id": "84:25/q07", "question": "How does this verse fit the warnings and the sūra's wider movement?", "turns_on": "Which level of context is explained: the immediate threat, the sūra's structure, its link to the preceding sūra, or the earlier statement about the denier.", "positions": [{"id": "84:25/q07/p1", "position": "It contrasts threatened disbelievers with believers receiving glad tidings and reward.", "reasons": "Kashifī, reported by Bursawī, says the threat also hints at believers' bodily and spiritual comfort. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the reward answers how believers fare after sarcastic glad tidings to the damned. Iṣlāḥī contrasts those adamantly rejecting the Qur'an with believers, then says the Prophet should warn those enslaved to worldly love, while faith and good works bring salvation and eternal reward. The Study Quran describes the ending as the different fates of believers and disbelievers, and reads 'but' in 84:25 as marking that contrast. Ṭabāṭabāʾī places the promise after the command to announce punishment."}, {"id": "84:25/q07/p2", "position": "The close continues al-Muṭaffifīn's contrast of rewarded allies and punished enemies who denied resurrection and judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī relates the sūra to the close of al-Muṭaffifīn and mentions 83:1, identifying their Creator-King as judge."}, {"id": "84:25/q07/p3", "position": "The sūra moves from Judgment Day events through contrasting reckonings and oaths to the two groups' final ends.", "reasons": "The Study Quran gives this outline of the sūra."}, {"id": "84:25/q07/p4", "position": "The nearby statement that God sees the denier answers his belief that he will not return: he will return and be requited.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives two formulations: God sees and requites his deeds, or God sees his state in the Hereafter and recompenses him."}]}
{"id": "84:25/q08", "question": "Where does the reward phrase or its root recur in the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:25/q08/p1", "position": "The reward phrase recurs in al-Qalam, Fuṣṣilat, al-Inshiqāq, and al-Tīn, with related uses of the root elsewhere.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ lists those reward passages, counts sixteen occurrences of the root mann, and notes r-rayb al-manūn at 52:30. Al-Samīn directs the reader to his explanation at 41:8; al-Dāmghānī and the Study Quran connect this verse to 41:8 and 95:6."}]}
{"id": "84:25/q09", "question": "What Prophetic virtue is reported for reading al-Inshiqāq?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "84:25/q09/p1", "position": "Its reader will be spared receiving their book from behind their back.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī transmits this as a Prophetic report."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q01", "question": "What does al-fajr mean as an Arabic word?", "turns_on": "Whether splitting is the root idea or an instance of a broader emergence.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q01/p1", "position": "Morning light breaking from night, or the time when it appears.", "reasons": "Tustari gives the outward sense as morning. Zajjaj, Mawardi, Tabarisi, Ibn Jawzi and Bint al-Shati describe darkness cleft by light. Ibn Jawzi relates the root to water bursting out and fājir breaking from obedience. Bint al-Shati cites six Quranic dawn uses, 2:187's white thread and 17:78's sequence after night; she also explains ghasaq as darkness mingled with first morning light or lingering evening light. Islahi distinguishes fajr's transition from subh, which extends beyond sunrise and is qualified in oaths (74:34; 81:18). Kuran Yolu gives brightness or daybreak time. Damghani glosses al-fajr simply as dawn. Mawardi describes light breaking over the eastern horizon, distinguishes the vanishing upright false dawn from the horizontally spreading true dawn, and cites a poet calling the latter truthful. Alusi derives the name from splitting the night and also glosses it as dawn's column or spreading light. Ibn Ashur describes the first eastern solar ray pushing back darkness before sunrise."}, {"id": "89:1/q01/p2", "position": "The root broadly denotes emergence or outburst, physically or figuratively.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati prefers this to al-Raghib's narrower splitting derivation. She cites springs, gushing and volcanoes, metaphorical emergence in goodness, generosity or evil, and the four pre-Islamic Fijar battle days. She counts 24 Quranic root uses, ten verbs mostly about water; 75:5 is the sole non-water verb. Nouns name rivers in 17:91, a spring in 76:6, and wickedness opposite piety in 91:8 and other passages."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q02", "question": "What color is the light called fajr?", "turns_on": "The Kufan and Medinan grammarians give different colors; the latter invoke garment usage.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q02/p1", "position": "White.", "reasons": "The Kufan grammarians call it whiteness; Elmalili describes first whiteness and Bint al-Shati cites 2:187's white thread."}, {"id": "89:1/q02/p2", "position": "Red.", "reasons": "The Medinan grammarians cite Arab usage for a red-dyed garment."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q03", "question": "What does al-fajr designate in the oath?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun denotes daily dawn, a whole day or prayer, a particular date or place, or a bursting spring or other emergence.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q03/p1", "position": "The familiar dawn occurring every day, taken generally.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas locates it in the east; al-Qurazi extends it daily until the world's end. Razi's Ibn Abbas report includes true and false dawn and says light ends night, sends creatures to provision and pictures resurrection (74:34; 81:18; 6:96). Alusi especially favors true dawn for its prayer and fasting role. Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and Tabatabai prefer generic dawn; Ibn Ashur cites its coordination with night. Elmalili calls it the joyful move into light (81:18). Bint al-Shati uses 2:187 against extending it to the whole day; Muhammad Abduh likewise treats dawn and the ten nights generically. Baydawi compares 81:18 and Nasafi 74:34. Al-Suyuti identifies the oath's dawn as the beginning of the day. Tabari holds that the oath denotes morning dawn; Mawardi reports Ali's daily morning view. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan call daily dawn the majority view; Ibn Kathir adds Ali, Mujahid and al-Suddi among its proponents. Durr says al-Hakim authenticated Ibn Abbas's general-daybreak report. Alusi prefers true dawn because prayer and fasting attach to it. Ibn Ashur says the generic article best fits the coordinated night in 89:4 and reports Qatada identifying the daily dawn-prayer time."}, {"id": "89:1/q03/p2", "position": "The dawn of Sacrifice Day, the tenth of Dhu al-Hijja.", "reasons": "Mujahid excludes every ordinary dawn. Abu Muslim links it to offerings and the ten nights' culmination. Razi recalls Abrahamic rites and 37:107. Qurtubi says pilgrimage remains valid until this dawn and reports the last of the ten as pilgrims leave Jam. Biqai mentions entering the sanctuary, ending consecration and divine hospitality; Bursevi lists circumambulation, shaving and stoning. Elmalili favors the collective joy of a particular feast, while generic dawn includes it; he reports Tabari endorsing Jabir's ten-of-sacrifice report on exegetical agreement. Study Quran cites 2:196-197 and 22:27-29. Ibn Kathir also attributes this view to Masruq and Muhammad ibn Kab, as the close of the ten nights. Qurtubi's Ibn Abbas report says this day has no night before or after and that a pilgrim reaching the standing place after Arafah still catches the pilgrimage until this dawn. Biqai calls it the complete dawn, magnified as though no other dawn existed. Ibn Ashur says its article would indicate a previously known day and locates the pilgrims at Muzdalifa. Durr's Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Kab reports expressly exclude every dawn."}, {"id": "89:1/q03/p3", "position": "The dawn prayer, in some reports including its Quran recitation.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports run through Atiyya and others. Ibn Atiyya adds Zayd ibn Aslam and dawn's Quran. Razi says night and day angels gather to hear it (17:78). Ibn Kathir also reports Ikrima. Samin explains the sense through an omitted noun. Tabatabai calls such proposals poor. Baghawi specifies Atiyya's transmission from Ibn Abbas. Razi argues that the prayer gathers night and day angels and that 17:78 describes its recitation as witnessed. Ibn Kathir also attributes the prayer reading to Ikrima. Alusi allows either an omitted noun or figuratively naming the prayer itself."}, {"id": "89:1/q03/p4", "position": "The first dawn of Muharram, opening the year.", "reasons": "Qatada calls it the year's first day; Qurtubi says the year then begins to emerge. Razi cites Muharram as God's greatest month and Ibn Abbas calling it the year's dawn, with recurring annual rites. Study Quran joins it to Muharram's first ten nights. Bursevi's Tabyan says New Year. Razi associates the first day with recurring observances and lunar reckoning and reports Ibn Abbas calling Muharram the year's dawn. Qurtubi specifies a chain through Atiyya and Ibn Muhaysin for Ibn Abbas's report. Alusi identifies Said ibn Mansur and Bayhaqi's al-Shuab as transmitters of the Ibn Abbas report."}, {"id": "89:1/q03/p5", "position": "The whole daytime, named for its beginning.", "reasons": "Repeated Ibn Abbas reports give the view. Mawardi and Ibn Jawzi explicitly explain part-for-whole naming; Razi compares 93:1 and 92:2. Bint al-Shati rejects it for night-ending dawn (2:187), and Tabatabai calls such proposals poor. Mawardi and Qurtubi explain naming the entire daytime by its beginning. Razi compares the oaths by forenoon and by day as it becomes clear (93:1; 92:2)."}, {"id": "89:1/q03/p6", "position": "The first dawn of Dhu al-Hijja.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak ties it to the ten nights; Ibn Jawzi specifies first day. Razi says the month opens great pilgrimage worship. Bint al-Shati reports Ibn al-Qayyim arguing from the following ten-night oath. Baghawi and Qurtubi transmit al-Dahhak's infer

{"id": "89:1/q04", "question": "Which dawn governs prayer and fasting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q04/p1", "position": "The horizontal true dawn; the earlier vertical false dawn is legally night.", "reasons": "Mawardi says the first narrow streak misleads and cites poetic al-musaddaq for truthful dawn. Jishumi, Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalili assign prayer and fasting rules only to spreading true dawn; Bursevi compares false dawn to a wolf's tail. Tabarisi distinguishes the two. Alusi says the legal role makes true dawn especially apt for the oath. Mawardi describes false dawn as an upright, narrow column that vanishes, leaving darkness before morning, and calls it misleading or the herald of morning; true dawn spreads horizontally and truthfully announces morning. Alusi says this legal distinction makes true dawn likelier as the oath's referent."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q05", "question": "How is the oath phrase grammatically construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the sworn object is named directly or an omitted head noun is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q05/p1", "position": "The oath wāw governs al-fajr in the genitive, directly swearing by dawn.", "reasons": "Nahhas gives the case analysis. Ibn al-Zubayr reports that God swears by dawn; Qurtubi counts five oaths. Ibn Ashur supplies the implicit oath verb, 'I swear by the dawn.' Bint al-Shati notes that oath-waw leads a clause to authenticate what is denied or mark acknowledgment and testimony. Tabari and Durr transmit Ibn al-Zubayr's statement that God swears by dawn; Qurtubi counts five oaths in the opening passage."}, {"id": "89:1/q05/p2", "position": "An omitted noun makes it an oath by the Lord of dawn.", "reasons": "Samin reports this; Bint al-Shati attributes supplied genitives to Tabari, Naysaburi and Zamakhshari."}, {"id": "89:1/q05/p3", "position": "An omitted noun makes it an oath by dawn prayer or Quran of dawn.", "reasons": "Samin gives prayer and Bint al-Shati reports Quran of dawn as another completion. Alusi permits supplying an omitted noun for the dawn prayer, alongside a figurative construal naming the prayer itself."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q06", "question": "Who may swear by a created dawn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q06/p1", "position": "God may swear by any created thing; humans may swear only by God.", "reasons": "Maymun ibn Mihran draws this rule from the divine oath. Durr transmits Maymun ibn Mihran's contrast between God's freedom to swear by any creation and the human restriction to swearing by God."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q07", "question": "Is al-fajr recited with verse-final tanwin?", "turns_on": "Whether verse endings are pronounced like poetic pauses; grammarians also dispute the form's name.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q07/p1", "position": "Most readers leave al-fajr without tanwin.", "reasons": "Samin says they likewise leave al-watr and yasr without it."}, {"id": "89:1/q07/p2", "position": "Abu al-Dinar al-Aʿrabi adds poetic pausal tanwin to al-fajr, al-watr and yasr.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says it substitutes for a lengthening letter and also reports Ibn Abbas's separate annexed layālin ʿashr. Abu Hayyan adduces a poem and grammatical discussion of open rhyme and ordinary pause. Ibn Khalawayh calls it tanwin al-tarannum, even on verbs and definite nouns. Samin notes some prefer tanwin tark al-tarannum and distinguish disputed tanwin al-ghali on closed rhymes; he cites 33:66-67, 33:10 and 13:9. Abu Hayyan reports Abu al-Dinar's tanwin on al-fajr, al-watr and yasr; Ibn Khalawayh and an unnamed poet illustrate rhyme-ending tanwin even on verbs and definite forms. Abu Hayyan compares unrestricted rhyme without tarannum, two prose stopping patterns, and treatment of verse endings as rhymes."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q08", "question": "What is the answer to the opening oath?", "turns_on": "Whether verse 14 states the response, ensuing stories imply an omitted one, or the preceding sura supplies one.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q08/p1", "position": "The expressed answer is that the Lord is surely watchful (89:14).", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Tabarisi, Ibn al-Anbari and Razi identify it; Bint al-Shati reports Razi treating intervening material as parenthetical. Ibn Masud says the oaths affirm watchfulness. Kuran Yolu adds knowledge of deeds and requital."}, {"id": "89:1/q08/p2", "position": "An unstated answer implies resurrection, judgment, punishment or requital.", "reasons": "Tabarisi suggests seizing oppressors or vindicating victims. Samin infers each person's recompense from earlier peoples and reports Zamakhshari's 'He will surely punish' from 89:6 and 89:13. Kuran Yolu gives resurrection and judgment. Bint al-Shati reports Ibn al-Qayyim's implicit answer in what befell Abraham and Muhammad. Al-Suyuti says an oath answer can be omitted because its objects already indicate the assertion, making the expression more forceful and concise; he reads the great pilgrimage rites and humble worship in these times as implying the honor of what Muhammad and Abraham brought."}, {"id": "89:1/q08/p3", "position": "The omitted answer is the end of al-Ghashiya: return to God for reckoning.", "reasons": "Samin reports the Shaykh's appeal to 88:25-26. Bint al-Shati reports Abu Hayyan and Muhammad Abduh arguing from printed adjacency; she rejects this because al-Ghashiya was revealed 58 suras after al-Fajr."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q09", "question": "Why is dawn chosen as an oath sign?", "turns_on": "The sources stress divine order, resurrection, particular rites, moral symbolism and the oaths' evidentiary role.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q09/p1", "position": "Its ordered light and benefit show the Creator's sole power.", "reasons": "Jishumi calls these signs proof of the Creator; Razi notes that dawn sends people and animals seeking provision. Islahi says God alone brings forth and removes, grants respite and harmonizes opposing forces (21:22); 28:71-72 illustrates His power over perpetual night or day. Elmalili sees changing time as lordship. Qutb portrays creation joyfully waking and praying. Corpus Coranicum cites a likely authentic Umayya poem greeting the Lord each dawn, suggesting a cultic connotation. Razi says oath objects have religious benefit as signs of oneness, worldly benefit calling for thanks, or both; their perceived priority drives interpretations. He links dawn to 74:34, 81:18 and God as maker of daybreak (6:96). Ibn Ashur calls the first light a display of divine power and artistry; it releases people from death-like sleep into aware, useful work. He says the times sworn by display God's craftsmanship and include times of worship."}, {"id": "89:1/q09/p2", "position": "Its daily return after dark images resurrection and judgment.", "reasons": "Razi and Bursevi compare dawn's spreading life with rising again. Biqai likens waking from sleep's lesser death to return, work and eventual recompense. Islahi invokes a waking supplication, 74:32-34, moral incompleteness without judgment and 68:35-36; ease and hardship prepare for 89:28. Kuran Yolu cites waking living things and 81:18. Razi compares creatures emerging at dawn with the dead rising from graves and calls it a lesson for reflection. Biqai says night and day renewing after disappearance demonstrate the power to resurrect. Ibn Ashur compares the end of sleep with a return from death."}, {"id": "89:1/q09/p3", "position": "The particular pilgrimage dawn carries collective joy and major rites.", "reasons": "Elmalili prefers its collective joy; the Dhu al-Hijja nights, Arafah and sacrifice sequence fits the sura and urges worship during limited life. Biqai mentions entry to the sanctuary and release from consecration; Bursevi cites Arafah supplication and Adha rites; Qurtubi links the dawn to pilgrimage completion. Corpus Coranicum finds a cultic ten-night interpretation persuasive despite objections to Neuwirth's liturgical reading. Al-Suyuti says these times

 contain the great rites of pilgrimage and humble worship, pointing to the honor of what Muhammad and Abraham brought. Razi explains the Day of Sacrifice's offering as a substitute for self-sacrifice the worshipper cannot make, citing 37:107. Biqai evokes return to the Sacred House, release from consecration and divine hospitality, and describes this dawn as complete and singularly grand."}, {"id": "89:1/q09/p4", "position": "Darkness yielding to light prompts moral reflection and repentance.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reads dawn, crescent and night as truth emerging after tyranny, with wealth and poverty tests and the tyrants' and tranquil soul's outcomes to follow. Bursevi urges washing sins with tears. Qutb pictures a joyful waking creation. Bint al-Shati reports Zamakhshari's admonitory reading of 89:6 and 89:14."}, {"id": "89:1/q09/p5", "position": "The oath objects are evidence for the sura's claim.", "reasons": "Islahi says identify the claim and compare parallel Quranic passages. Bint al-Shati rejects making every object a symbol of honor; she reports Tabari's caution against unsupported interpretation and Razi's and Zamakhshari's criticism of speculation. Elmalili notes disagreement on definiteness, article scope and oath objects. Bint al-Shati argues that discerning a created thing's purpose does not establish its greatness; interpreters must attend to restrictive wording such as 'when it settles' or 'when it falls.' She asks what oath-waw conveys to an Arab listener beyond an explicit 'I swear by' construction. Ibn Ashur says an oath calls God to witness an assertion; God's own oaths serve to confirm that assertion."}, {"id": "89:1/q09/p6", "position": "The oath magnifies the thing sworn by, inviting inquiry into its greatness.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports this as the view of most exegetes."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q10", "question": "How does dawn relate to the following and parallel oaths?", "turns_on": "The next oath supports different calendars; other sources read the series through cosmic contrasts.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q10/p1", "position": "Dawn and departing night are the chief contrast; intervening oaths develop it.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the blessed ten are a subset of night. Corpus Coranicum compares 74:34, 81:18, 91:1-3, 92:2 and 93:1 and notes that the ten uniquely quantify night. Islahi calls first and last primary and the middle secondary. Tabatabai glosses dawn, even, odd and withdrawing night; al-Aswad pairs familiar dawn with Dhu al-Hijja's ten. Ibn Ashur connects dawn's transition from darkness with the fully dark night and says generic dawn best suits its coordination with night in 89:4; the other sworn times are also associated with worship."}, {"id": "89:1/q10/p2", "position": "Cosmic oppositions anticipate moral oppositions and final recompense.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum compares 91:9-10 and 92:4-10, plus similar oath openings in 91-93, 95, 100 and 103. Bint al-Shati sees truth after tyranny; Islahi says worldly pairs call for an afterlife settling good and evil."}, {"id": "89:1/q10/p3", "position": "The formula resembles Quranic oaths and may echo pre-Islamic soothsayer language.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum calls the soothsayer link probable but under-studied, compares 100:1-5, points to discussion of 93:1-2 and lists similar sura openings. Islahi compares receding night and appearing morning in 74:32-34. Al-Zarkashi and al-Suyuti each count fifteen suras beginning with an oath, including al-Fajr, and classify oath as the fifth form of sura opening."}, {"id": "89:1/q10/p4", "position": "Dawn and ten nights point to Dhu al-Hijja and sacrifice rites.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak and Ibn al-Qayyim argue from the next oath. A Jabir report identifies the dawn and ten with the ten of sacrifice; Elmalili reports Tabari endorsing it and prefers the ten nights, Arafah and Sacrifice Day sequence. Baghawi and Qurtubi report al-Dahhak arguing from the neighboring ten-night oath (89:2); Razi adds that the first dawn opens the month of pilgrimage."}, {"id": "89:1/q10/p5", "position": "Dawn and ten nights point to Muharram's first days.", "reasons": "Study Quran explicitly pairs Muharram's beginning and ten nights; Qatada calls it the year's first day."}, {"id": "89:1/q10/p6", "position": "Dawn and ten nights point to Ramadan's final ten and first revelation.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 97:1."}, {"id": "89:1/q10/p7", "position": "The extended oath sequence builds anticipation for its eventual assertion.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the accumulated oaths make the listener await the statement they confirm."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q11", "question": "How does this opening connect to the sura and al-Ghashiya?", "turns_on": "The sources stress judgment, moral testing, divine power and the basmala.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q11/p1", "position": "It supports return, reckoning and divine watchfulness announced at al-Ghashiya's end.", "reasons": "Jishumi links the prior chapter's return and judgment to this chapter's warning and encouragement. Biqai repeatedly cites 88:26, waking from death-like sleep and work before recompense; pilgrimage clothing, talbiya and sacred travel evoke resurrection. Islahi says the prior signs of divine power, wisdom and providence require accountability. Alusi reports Suyuti's view that the oath affirms al-Ghashiya's promise and threat and parallels its opening questions. Abu Hayyan relates the earlier warning against turning away and disbelief to the later warning that God lies in wait (citing 92:16 and 89:14). Biqai reads pilgrimage clothing, talbiya and journey to appointed places as reminders of return and resurrection. Alusi transmits Suyuti's comparison between the openings' questions, including 88:17."}, {"id": "89:1/q11/p2", "position": "It prepares tyrants' stories, human tests and the tranquil soul at judgment.", "reasons": "Alusi connects al-Ghashiya's two classes of faces (88:2, 88:8) with deniers and the blessed soul (89:27). Study Quran traces oaths, tyrants, fortune, stinginess and judgment. Tabatabai says worldly attachment causes tyranny and ingratitude; wealth and poverty test preparation for the next life, while the tranquil soul stays submitted through gain and loss. Bint al-Shati anticipates these oppositions in the natural contrasts. Qutb describes Meccan scenes, rhythms, rhyme, warning, history and moral correction. Abu Hayyan connects al-Ghashiya's downcast and radiant faces (88:2, 88:8) with the deniers and tranquil soul (89:27); Alusi also follows that contrast. Ibn Ashur says the sura warns Meccan polytheists through Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, promises the Prophet his enemies' decline, and refutes treating prosperity as divine honor and believers' poverty as humiliation; failure to share and greed lead to regret over neglecting faith and good works."}, {"id": "89:1/q11/p3", "position": "The signs establish sole divine rule and the need for a just afterlife.", "reasons": "Islahi says the Prophet warns through heavenly and earthly signs even when some cannot see; harmonized opposites require one sovereign (21:22), and unrequited good and evil would make creation purposeless (68:35-36). Alternating day and night show even the powerful cannot escape God (28:71-72)."}, {"id": "89:1/q11/p4", "position": "The basmala evokes mercy, lovers' self-offering and gathering at resurrection.", "reasons": "Qushayri says reciting satisfies worshippers while lovers offer life; the basmala unsettles the poor, disorients the enamored and brings mercy to lovers. Biqai portrays God reassembling dispersed people, giving guidance and granting His allies contentment and gardens."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q12", "question": "What inward meaning is given to dawn?", "turns_on": "These readings transpose dawn's light to prophetic, devotional and eschatological experience.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q12/p1", "position": "Muhammad, through whom faith and obedience shine and unbelief disappears.", "reasons": "Tustari adds the lights of both worlds; Ibn Ata as reported by Sulami stresses faith dispelling unbelief."}, {"id": "89:1/q12/p2", "position": "At the great resurrection, divine light appearing in the soul's night.", "reasons": "Qashani relates ten to dormant senses during disclosure, pair to witness and witnessed, odd to oneness after duality and night to disappearing selfhood."}, {"id": "89:1/q12/p3", "position": "At death's lesser resurrection, the sun rising from the west.", "reasons": "Qashani relates ten to dimmed senses, pair to spirit and body, odd to separated spirit and night to bodily darkness dispersing."}, {"id": "89:1/q12/p4", "position": "The saints' opening worship or lovers' communion with God.", "reasons": "Qushayri reports the former and Kashifi through Bursevi the latter."}]}

{"id": "89:1/q14", "question": "What reports concern reciting Surat al-Fajr?", "turns_on": "The reports describe distinct merits and uses.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q14/p1", "position": "Recitation brings forgiveness; daily recitation brings light on Resurrection Day.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits the attributed Prophetic promise through Ubayy ibn Kab."}, {"id": "89:1/q14/p2", "position": "The Prophet recommended it among short suras for communal prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Durr recount a worshipper leaving Muadh's long prayer and the Prophet rebuking Muadh for driving people away; the suggested chapters also include 87:1, 91:1 and 92:1. Ibn Kathir and Durr transmit Jabir's account of the Prophet rebuking Muadh for lengthening prayer and suggesting al-Fajr among shorter suras, alongside al-Ala, al-Shams and al-Layl."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q15", "question": "What Muharram and Ashura reports accompany this dawn interpretation?", "turns_on": "These are distinct accompanying reports; the eye-treatment report is explicitly weakened.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q15/p1", "position": "Muharram and Ashura are especially recommended for fasting.", "reasons": "Durr reports the Prophet calling Muharram God's month and best for fasting after Ramadan, with night prayer best after obligatory prayer. Ali recommends Muharram because of repentance and forgiveness. Reports commend an adjacent day to Ashura or ninth and tenth to differ from Jews. Ibn Shihab fasted while traveling because Ashura would pass; Abu Musa and Abu Hurayra connect its fast to Jewish festivity and prophets' practice. Durr reports Muharram as the best voluntary fasting month after Ramadan, with night prayer best after obligatory prayer; another report recalls a day of repentance and forgiveness. Ashura reports recount Moses' rescue, the Prophet's order to fast, Ansar families helping children fast with wool toys, and Ibn Abbas's special esteem for its fast. Al-Aswad says only Ali and Abu Musa among Kufan Companions urged it. Reports propose fasting the ninth, the day before or after, or both adjacent days to differ from Jews. Ibn Shihab fasted it while traveling because its opportunity cannot be made up; Abu Musa mentions the Jewish festival and Abu Hurayra the prophets' practice."}, {"id": "89:1/q15/p2", "position": "Generosity to one's family on Ashura brings provision through the year.", "reasons": "Durr gives reports through Jabir, Ibn Masud, Abu Said and Abu Hurayra and a traditional saying; Bayhaqi says individually weak chains support one another. Durr supplies reports through Jabir, Ibn Masud, Abu Said and Abu Hurayra, as well as Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Muntashir's reported saying. Al-Bayhaqi regards the separate weak chains as mutually strengthening."}, {"id": "89:1/q15/p3", "position": "Antimony on the eyes on Ashura prevents inflammation forever.", "reasons": "Durr reports it through Urwa from Ibn Abbas and notes Bayhaqi weakened it. Durr transmits the promise through Ibn Abbas and notes Bayhaqi's judgment that it is weak."}, {"id": "89:1/q15/p4", "position": "Muharram is called God's greatest month.", "reasons": "Razi relays an unnamed report using this description without supplying a chain or grading."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q16", "question": "What do attached reports say the ten nights, even and odd denote?", "turns_on": "They differ over even and odd: pilgrimage days or creation and God.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q16/p1", "position": "The ten are Dhu al-Hijja's first ten, odd is Arafah and even is Sacrifice Day.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Durr transmit Jabir's report from the Prophet."}, {"id": "89:1/q16/p2", "position": "The ten are the ten of sacrifice, even is created pairs and odd is God.", "reasons": "A report through Atiyya and Abu Said links pairs to 78:8 and God's oneness to 112:1; Durr gives a related report citing 78:8."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q17", "question": "How do poetic comparisons picture dawn against night?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q17/p1", "position": "Dawn appears as a small bright mark, band, or trim against a much wider dark field.", "reasons": "Jurjani says the resemblance to a horse's blaze, black silk's white mark, Ibn al-Mutazz's brocade, or trim on night rests on contrast, not equal size or brightness. He notes a poet's intensified ink-black night and compares the principle with sun, mirror, and coin similes that select shape, gleam, or color; such comparisons can be reversed."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q18", "question": "What does the Gabriel visit report say in the surrounding revelation discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q18/p1", "position": "Gabriel appeared to Umm Salama as Dihya al-Kalbi and was later identified by the Prophet.", "reasons": "Abu Uthman reports the visit from Usama ibn Zayd; Ibn Kathir says Bukhari and Muslim transmit additional routes."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q19", "question": "How is al-Fajr counted among short verses, and how are verse boundaries determined?", "turns_on": "Different counting conventions and judgments about the shortest verse.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q19/p1", "position": "Al-Fajr is a one-word verse and among the shortest verses, often paired with al-Duha.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi counts al-Fajr, al-Duha, and al-Asr as one-word verses, says al-Duha followed by al-Fajr is shortest, and compares one-word openings for verse-ending sound. Al-Suyuti reports an authority pairing al-Duha and al-Fajr as shortest. Ibn Ashur says al-Fajr implies an oath verb, so a verse can be complete by ellipsis."}, {"id": "89:1/q19/p2", "position": "'Then he looked' is shortest; Amma, al-Fajr, and al-Duha are equal in shortness.", "reasons": "Al-Mawsili gives this alternative ranking, reported by al-Suyuti."}, {"id": "89:1/q19/p3", "position": "Verse boundaries are transmitted, with differences arising from pauses and continuation.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi reports al-Zamakhshari saying boundaries are fixed by revelation rather than analogy, and says a prophetic pause could be mistaken for a boundary when he sometimes continued. Ibn Ashur says the Companions knew transmitted divisions but reports can differ over where adjoining verses divide; he compares conventionally counted opening letters."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q20", "question": "What is the shortest Quranic word, and what counts as a word?", "turns_on": "What is counted as an independent word.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q20/p1", "position": "The one-letter preposition bi is shorter than two-letter candidates.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi rejects al-Dani's two-letter minimum and notes that literal sense, figurative sense, written form, and convention can yield differing word counts; he otherwise describes a word as a single utterance of two to ten letters."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q21", "question": "How do sound and meaning govern the endings of al-Fajr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q21/p1", "position": "The endings may match in sound when the wording remains natural and led by meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi reports al-Zamakhshari's warning against sound ornament that distorts structure or exclusivity and says natural identical or close fawasil are praiseworthy; the ya in yasr is dropped for the endings. Bint al-Shati reports the same standard and al-Rummani's dispute over saj terminology, with al-Khafaji's explanation for calling such endings fawasil."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q22", "question": "How should al-fajr's consonants be articulated in recitation?", "turns_on": "The final ra changes with connected kasra and stopping.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q22/p1", "position": "Its jim exemplifies the strong, voiced qalqala consonants.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari says a quiescent ba and the other qalqala letters retain plosive strength and voicing; he names al-fajr as an example. His surrounding articulation discussion also treats emphatic alifs, smooth initial hamza, and light ba before emphatics."}, {"id": "89:1/q22/p2", "position": "Its final ra is light with kasra in connected speech, but emphatic at a stop is preferred.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari says every reader lightens a kasra-bearing ra, citing al-fajr, and prefers tafkhim when stopping on it. He contrasts ra with imala or intermediate reading against full fath and surveys moving, quiescent, rounded, and kasra-bearing ra; for other rounded ra after kasra or silent ya he reports competing emphatic and light treatments, preferring the latter, with disputed examples."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q23", "question": "What pause or basmala is used between al-Fajr and the following sura?", "turns_on": "The reader's usual practice in joining or pausing between suras.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q23/p1", "position": "Some readers who generally join suras make a brief pa

use at this transition.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari lists this among four transitions, to avoid awkward adjoining phrases such as 'Enter My garden, No'; special sakt presumes joining elsewhere."}, {"id": "89:1/q23/p2", "position": "Some readers who generally pause use the basmala at this transition.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari names Ibn Ghalbun, Makki, and others; he says special basmala presumes pausing elsewhere and cannot be inserted where transmitted joining excludes it."}, {"id": "89:1/q23/p3", "position": "Most authorities make no special exception for this transition.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari names Faris ibn Ahmad, Ibn Sufyan, Abu al-Tahir, the Iraqis, and al-Dani among those making no distinction."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q24", "question": "How long is the vowel when stopping with incidental sukun as in al-fajr?", "turns_on": "Whether stopping sukun counts like a necessary second sukun.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q24/p1", "position": "Fully extend it as a meeting of two sukuns.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari reports early Egyptian teachers through al-Dani, al-Shatibi's choice, and Ibn al-Fahham's exceptional full extension route from Hisham; he reasons that necessary-sukun madd receives full extension."}, {"id": "89:1/q24/p2", "position": "Use medium length because the stopping sukun is incidental.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari attributes this to Ibn Mujahid, his students, al-Dani, and other routes, balancing the two sukuns with the accidental pause."}, {"id": "89:1/q24/p3", "position": "Shorten it because the incidental stopping sukun does not count.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazari reports Abu al-Hasan al-Husri's view and examples al-qadr and al-fajr."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q25", "question": "Where does al-Fajr stand in codex ordering and textual-history reports?", "turns_on": "How reported personal codices relate to the received order and collection.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q25/p1", "position": "Codex reports place al-Fajr differently, while the present verse and sura order is held to be prophetic.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti reports Ibn Masud placing al-Fajr before al-Asr among the mufassal suras; Alusi gives a codex order placing it after al-Tahrim. He says Quranic material was memorized and separately written in the Prophet's lifetime, rejecting proof of a single bound codex then; he also reports disputed additional text and recitation reports."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q26", "question": "Is al-Fajr classified as containing abrogation?", "turns_on": "Whether the broad sura categories withstand the detailed abrogation cases.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q26/p1", "position": "One classification says it contains neither abrogating nor abrogated material.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti reports this classification, which places al-Asr in a different category containing both."}, {"id": "89:1/q26/p2", "position": "That four-part sura classification is open to question.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti rejects uncritical use of it; his surrounding discussion distinguishes several kinds of changed obligation and three kinds of abrogation, including the debated nursing report and cases where a ruling ends but recitation remains."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q27", "question": "What added-letter spelling conventions appear in the surrounding writing discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q27/p1", "position": "Some written alifs, yas, and waws are added by orthographic convention, perhaps reflecting older vowel notation.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti lists extra alifs after waw and certain hamzas, extra ya in specified phrases, and extra waw in ulu and related forms; he reports al-Kirmani's older-script explanation."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q28", "question": "Why are Quranic passages called ayat in the discussion that cites al-Fajr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q28/p1", "position": "An ayah is a transmitted Quranic unit and a sign of its inimitable revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says a Quranic portion can be explicitly complete, understood by ellipsis, or complete by inclusion; he calls ayah a Quranic designation grounded in the text's eloquence and challenge. {"id": "89:1/q29", "question": "How are disjoint-letter sura openings explained in the related opening-form discussion?", "turns_on": "Whether a later explicit mention of the Quran is needed.", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q29/p1", "position": "Their relation to later Quran references reflects the audience's attention and the weight of revelation.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports al-Razi's explanations that mentioning the Quran draws attention to all of it and that some openings reflect its obligations; she finds these explanations forced. Al-Zarkashi asks about exceptions to the usual later Quran mention."}, {"id": "89:1/q29/p2", "position": "Every disjoint-letter sura contains a defense of the Quran and its inimitability.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports Ibn Kathir's inductive explanation for the apparent exceptions."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q30", "question": "How is the sura titled in transmitted texts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q30/p1", "position": "Surat al-Fajr, without the opening oath waw.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says Quran copies, commentaries and hadith books consistently use this title."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q31", "question": "Can al-fajr and the neighboring oath terms have more than one referent?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q31/p1", "position": "Shared terms can denote multiple things, with either one or several senses intended.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti lists dawn, the ten nights, even and odd among examples of terms whose referents can be multiple; whether both senses are intended varies."}]}
{"id": "89:1/q32", "question": "Whom does the opening oath address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "89:1/q32/p1", "position": "The Prophet directly, while indirectly assuring deniers that the assertion will occur.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur infers the address to the Prophet from the later reminders of God's acts against Ad and of divine watchfulness (89:6, 89:14)."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q01", "question": "Who is the polytheist eligible to seek protection?", "turns_on": "Whether the indefinite 'one' specifies universal coverage and how the preceding fighting order bounds it.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q01/p1", "position": "Any individual polytheist covered by the fighting order, including a person from a hostile or treaty breaking group after the grace period.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq identifies those ordered fought; Ibn Abbas calls him treatyless; Ibn Ashur says 'one' makes coverage universal even after a broken pact, citing 5:2 and the ban on answering betrayal with betrayal. Al-Burhan argues from the grammar of an indefinite noun under a conditional particle that the example of any polytheist seeking protection has general scope."}, {"id": "9:6/q01/p2", "position": "The phrasing includes any polytheist who seeks to hear revelation or has a sound reason to visit.", "reasons": "Mujahid says whoever comes to hear the Prophet and revelation; al-Biqa'i calls it a limited middle course after general restrictions; Ibn Ashur stresses the individual noun and hypothetical conditional. Bint al-Shati identifies people who have not yet heard God's words as the intended listeners and says accomplished eloquence is no prerequisite."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q02", "question": "How is 'if one of the polytheists seeks protection' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the nominative is governed by a recovered verb or is an initial subject; why in permits the construction.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q02/p1", "position": "A hidden verb raises ahad, and istajāraka explains it; conditional in is normally followed by a verb.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash calls this the more analogical analysis; al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, al-Baydawi and others reject a bare subject after in. Al-Farra says in uniquely tolerates separation from its jussive verb; 4:176 and poetry illustrate it. Sibawayh calls in the mother of conditionals. Al-Burhan places this conditional construction among cases where an omitted verb is explained by another expression, comparing 'iyyāya fa-rhabūn' and 'wa-l-samāʾa rafaʿahā'."}, {"id": "9:6/q02/p2", "position": "Ahad can be a nominal subject after the conditional, with a following verbal predicate; the implied verb is only an analytical device.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash adduces noun-initial constructions after an, including poems 'ʿāwid Harāʾa', 'lā tajzaʿī', and 'atajzaʿ'; Abu Ali answers al-Zajjaj by invoking Sibawayh and an underlying verb in the response. Ibn Ashur appeals to generic indefiniteness and conditional generality."}, {"id": "9:6/q02/p3", "position": "The special grammar of in is not explained by saying it occurs only in conditions.", "reasons": "Ibn Yazid notes that in can mean mā, be extra, or be lightened from inna; its ambiguity remains distinctive. Al-Qurtubi transmits the same objection to Sibawayh."}]}

{"id": "9:6/q04", "question": "What force do the indefinite ahad and fronted conditional have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q04/p1", "position": "They foreground any individual seeker and strengthen the protection rule.", "reasons": "Sibawayh, as reported by Razi, sees fronting the important object as protecting blood despite the fight command. Ibn Jinni finds breadth in conditional in and allows ahad to mean one individual, citing 4:128 and 4:176. Al-Burhan adds expected occurrence and special identification; Ibn Ashur says the rare hypothetical precludes an excuse that access was denied. Al-Burhan gives the general Arabic rule that an indefinite noun under a conditional particle covers every instance, illustrating it with seeing any person and with this verse's seeker."}, {"id": "9:6/q04/p2", "position": "The doubled explanatory construction gives emphasis.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says an object or subject mentioned first and resumed by a pronoun or explanatory verb has greater force than ordinary order, citing 17:100, 76:31, 7:30, 82:1, and 84:1."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q05", "question": "What does istajāraka mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q05/p1", "position": "To ask for shelter, security or a protector.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi relates it to taking someone into one's neighborhood; Asad invokes the Arabian duty to protect neighbors. Ibn Ashur calls neighboring a metaphor from safe residence and says ajāra means securing rather than literally making a neighbor. Al-Tha'labi adduces Arabic usage and poetry."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q06", "question": "For what purposes does the verse require or allow safe conduct?", "turns_on": "Whether hearing God's speech defines the seeker's reason for asking or the host's purpose in granting refuge.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q06/p1", "position": "Protection to hear and examine Islam is obligatory; other purposes can also be protected according to their circumstances and Muslim interests.", "reasons": "Qurtubi calls religious inquiry the verse's apparent case and other grants matters of public interest. Elmalili distinguishes obligatory religious protection from context dependent worldly requests. Ibn Kathir lists missions, trade, peace, truce and tribute; Wahidi lists trade, envoys, and property retrieval. Ibn Ashur allows reasonable motives and says discussion of Islam will occur during a temporary stay. Malik would return an ambiguous enemy encountered on a road to safety, and Ibn al-Qasim applies the same protection to a coastal trader expecting peaceful sale. Ibn Ashur cites the Prophet's prohibition on betraying a betrayer."}, {"id": "9:6/q06/p2", "position": "The request itself is general, while hearing God's word is the grantor's purpose.", "reasons": "Elmalili prefers no restriction of the seeker to religious needs; Alusi says Ali's reported 'need' may be general, although he identifies its immediate case as religious."}, {"id": "9:6/q06/p3", "position": "The verse specifically protects a request for religious inquiry or a comparable religious need.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i denies that the verse establishes general asylum for unrelated reasons; Shaykh al-Islam ties the request to the stated end of hearing. Some interpreters read Ali's 'need' religiously."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q07", "question": "Who may grant effective safe conduct?", "turns_on": "Which persons can bind the community by a pledge and how to treat an ambiguous pledge.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q07/p1", "position": "The ruler, a free Muslim, a slave, a free woman, and a fighting capable minor may grant it.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says the ruler acts for the public benefit and all accept a free man's pledge; he prefers the majority's permission for a slave, citing the hadith that even the lowest Muslim grants protection, and says lack of a war stipend is immaterial. Abu Hayyan lists the Awza'i, Thawri, Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, Abu Thawr, Dawud and the known Maliki view; a fighting boy belongs to the defenders."}, {"id": "9:6/q07/p2", "position": "A slave's or woman's pledge needs the imam's review or approval; some deny the slave's pledge.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and another Maliki view deny a slave's effective pledge; Ibn Habib refers it to the imam. Ibn al-Majishun alone conditions a free woman's pledge on imam approval, which Abu Hayyan calls anomalous."}, {"id": "9:6/q07/p3", "position": "Even an ambiguous pledge by a child or insane person may protect the entrant pending safe return.", "reasons": "Wahidi's jurists treat a minor's or insane person's promise as ambiguous safe conduct; Elmalili reports protection for lawful religious and trade entrants even under such a guarantee."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q08", "question": "What does the command 'grant him protection' require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q08/p1", "position": "Secure the seeker from killing and attack while he hears the message, then preserve his safety until return.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj specifies protection from killing; al-Nahhas removes him from the kill order. Al-Biqa'i requires protection against anyone who might harm him; Kuranyolu stresses absence of fear and pressure."}, {"id": "9:6/q08/p2", "position": "A treatyless arrival can either be received or returned safely.", "reasons": "Aṭāʾ's report leaves the two practical dispositions open."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q09", "question": "How long may the protection last?", "turns_on": "Whether a fixed four month interval governs or the ruler and circumstances determine the stay.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q09/p1", "position": "It continues through genuine inquiry and until the visitor reaches safety; its exact duration is set by circumstances or the ruler.", "reasons": "Razi says custom governs, continuing while truth seeking is sincere but not for a deceptive delay.
